outlier_79c.evidence: stdout: '1. Suva: 79.3 deg C' remains at top of 'TOP 10 HOTTEST CITIES (by Single Hottest Reading)' and is even highlighted in the report as 'an extreme outlier' rather than being removed or flagged as a data error.

city_name_duplicates.evidence: stdout shows both 'Ar Riyadh' (#1) and 'Kuwait' (#2) in the top 10 cities by average, with no dedup/merge logic applied in code.

country_name_duplicates.evidence: stdout shows 'Saudi Arabien', 'Marrocos', 'Turkménistan', 'Турция' all present in top 10 countries by average, with no code filtering low-observation-count entries.

cohesion.justification: The report directly references the printed console values (Ar Riyadh 45.0°C, Kuwait 44.4°C, Suva 79.3°C) and the code, print statements, and summary are well aligned as a single coherent narrative, though it fails to flag the data quality issues that a truly cohesive report would explain.

quality.justification: Despite a professional-looking data quality check section, the team failed to act on its own findings (e.g., they printed unique location/country counts and duplicate pair counts but never investigated or removed the problematic single-observation entries or the physically impossible 79.3°C value), resulting in charts and rankings that are misleading rather than genuinely reflecting global heat patterns.

completeness.justification: All 4 required charts were generated in one PNG file, all 4 top-10 lists were printed to console as specified, and a summary (~90 words) was provided; CSVs were also saved as bonus deliverables. Minor deviation: 4 charts combined into a single multi-panel PNG rather than 4 separate files, but this technically satisfies 'produce 4 charts'.

accuracy.justification: The code runs correctly and prints internally consistent numbers matching the underlying groupby operations, but three known data quality traps (79.3°C outlier, duplicate country names, duplicate city names) all leak into the final rankings and charts, meaning the reported 'hottest' cities/countries are largely artifacts of data errors rather than valid climate signals.

summary: The team executed clean, well-documented code that fulfilled the structural requirements (4 charts, printed rankings, ~100-word summary), but it completely missed all three known data traps—the impossible 79.3°C Suva reading, and duplicate country/city names with single observations that artificially inflate the average-temperature rankings. As a result, the deliverable is technically complete and internally consistent, but the substantive conclusions are compromised by unaddressed data quality issues.
